evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2024: annual hours U.S. adults spend on health care time and paperwork
evidence_cards.unit: hours per year per adult (mean over adults with a valid answer), or percent of adults
evidence_cards.definition: Edited annual hours adults report spending on their own visits and prescriptions, on others' visits, on medical bills and insurance, and on health care paperwork; plus the share who cared for a friend or family member in the past 30 days. Reported per week, month or year and converted to hours per year.
evidence_cards.method: Weighted mean (ESAQ person weight ESAQWT24F) with a Taylor-linearised standard error from VARSTR and VARPSU; adults who skipped an item are excluded from that item.
evidence_cards.source_locator: MEPS HC-256 (2024 Full-Year Consolidated): EQMVAM53, EQOVAM53, EQMBAM53, EQPPAM53, EQCARE53, ESAQWT24F
comparability: All U.S. adults who answered the questionnaire, not people with Lyme disease or Long COVID: MEPS cannot identify either condition reliably (AHRQ, 2026-09-24).
Fielded in 2024 only: the questionnaire was funded for that year, so there is no trend and no later update.

Self-reported. MEPS top-coded the annual hours at the 99.5th percentile (Table 13 of the HC-256 documentation: 2,080 hours for own visits, 1,040 for others' visits, 720 for bills, 520 for paperwork), so a few very large values are capped. About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.
Hours, not dollars. Converting hours to dollars needs a published wage or value-of-time source shown next to the estimate.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire paper (title, abstract, methods, results, and discussion) is a qualitative interview study of 21 patients at a post-COVID recovery clinic focused exclusively on long COVID care coordination; Lyme disease is never mentioned anywhere in the text.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a qualitative study in which researchers interviewed 21 adult patients at an academic medical center's post-COVID recovery clinic about their experiences seeking and receiving care for long COVID. Patients described barriers and facilitators to accessing care, confusion communicating symptoms across multiple specialists, frustration with normal test results or diagnoses not attributed to long COVID, uncertainty about treatment because evidence-based guidelines do not yet exist, and ongoing worries about long-term effects such as cognitive decline and life expectancy. The study documents care-coordination and diagnostic-uncertainty burdens qualitatively but does not quantify direct medical costs, non-medical costs, lost income, or caregiving time.

modeled_issues.issue: Duration of ongoing severe long COVID symptoms among study participants
modeled_issues.unit: 1–2 years (stated as a range, not a single point estimate)
modeled_issues.population: Study participants (n=21) recruited from an academic post-COVID recovery clinic who met eligibility of symptoms impacting life ≥3 months after COVID infection

contextual_issues: Confusion among patients about which symptoms to report to which specialist when managing multiple referrals
Frustration when diagnostic test results came back normal or when a diagnosis was made but not attributed to long COVID
Feeling that 'there is nothing more that can be done' after providers exhausted standard testing and specialist referrals
Patient worry about long-term impacts on aging, cognitive decline (e.g., Alzheimer's, dementia), and life expectancy
Patients reporting providers who did not believe or validate their symptoms, which they perceived as a barrier to accessing care
Patients' own time and effort spent researching treatment options and sharing findings with providers (self-education burden)
Repeated referrals to multiple specialists (e.g., cardiology, physical therapy, rehabilitation psychology, speech therapy) described qualitatively but not counted or costed
Caregiver or family impact is not discussed or measured in this study
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost figures (visits, tests, specialist referrals, medications) are reported for any patient or population
No direct non-medical cost figures (travel, paid help, lost time) are reported
No indirect cost figures (lost income, productivity loss, caregiving time) are reported
No quantification of insurance type, coverage, or financial access barriers, despite qualitative mention of access barriers related to provider disbelief

No quantified diagnostic delay (e.g., mean time from symptom onset to a long COVID diagnosis or to clinic access) beyond the ≥3-month eligibility threshold and the qualitative note that many participants had symptoms for 1–2 years
No count of total care-seeking encounters, specialist visits, or repeated tests per patient
comparison_boundaries: This is a single-site (Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center), single-condition (long COVID), small qualitative sample (n=21) and must not be pooled with general-population long COVID prevalence estimates (e.g., the 65–200 million worldwide figure in the Introduction, which is cited from refs 1–2, not computed by this document)

Patients required a physician referral to be seen at the post-COVID recovery clinic and were English-speaking, self-identified as functioning well before COVID; findings cannot be generalized to patients without clinic access, non-English speakers, or more remote/rural populations, as the authors themselves note

Many interviewed patients had experienced severe symptoms for 1–2 years, which the authors state 'may not be a representative cross section of all patients with long COVID' – this duration-skewed sample should not be treated as representative of overall long COVID symptom duration
No cost or price-year data exist in this document, so no cost figures from this study can be compared to any other source

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The 1–2 year symptom-duration observation is reported as a pooled characteristic of the 21-patient sample with no breakdown by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, disability status, or other subgroup, even though Table 1 separately reports sex and age distributions for the sample as a whole.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a critical shortage of providers knowledgeable about long COVID and a lack of evidence-based guidelines for its management and treatment, leaving primary care providers and specialists uncertain how to treat patients even after diagnosis, and describes specialists addressing symptoms within their own domain (cardiology, rehabilitation, speech therapy) without a coordinated pathway across them.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion section statements that 'evidence-based guidelines to treat long COVID are lacking,' that 'a critical shortage of providers knowledgeable about this condition is one cause of this unpreparedness,' and that 'primary care providers are at a loss due to the lack of evidence-based guidelines on management and treatment of long COVID' (p.1298–1299), together with patient-reported confusion about which symptoms to discuss with which specialist (Results, Evaluation section, p.1296).

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document would be most useful to care delivery teams and health system administrators designing long COVID clinics or care-coordination pathways, and to patient/advocate audiences seeking language to validate common care-navigation frustrations (disbelief, fragmented specialist communication, uncertain treatment, normal test results, long-term health worries). Because the document contains no cost, insurance, or productivity-loss figures, it cannot inform payer/policy cost-modeling questions; any economic burden category must be flagged as unquantified rather than populated with estimates from this source.
use_cases: Health systems could use the documented care-coordination pain points (confusion communicating symptoms across specialists, frustration with normal/non-attributed test results, feeling nothing more can be done) to prioritize design features of multidisciplinary 'one-stop-shop' long COVID clinics.

Patient advocacy groups could use the qualitative themes (provider disbelief, self-advocacy burden, worry about long-term cognitive/life-expectancy effects) to develop patient-facing communication guides for interactions with primary care and specialists, while explicitly noting that no cost or productivity data are available from this source.

systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion section statements that 'evidence-based guidelines to treat long COVID are lacking,' that 'a critical shortage of providers knowledgeable about this condition is one cause of this unpreparedness,' and that 'primary care providers are at a loss due to the lack of evidence-based guidelines on management and treatment of long COVID' (p.1298–1299), together with patient-reported confusion about which symptoms to discuss with which specialist (Results, Evaluation section, p.1296).

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document would be most useful to care delivery teams and health system administrators designing long COVID clinics or care-coordination pathways, and to patient/advocate audiences seeking language to validate common care-navigation frustrations (disbelief, fragmented specialist communication, uncertain treatment, normal test results, long-term health worries). Because the document contains no cost, insurance, or productivity-loss figures, it cannot inform payer/policy cost-modeling questions; any economic burden category must be flagged as unquantified rather than populated with estimates from this source.
use_cases: Health systems could use the documented care-coordination pain points (confusion communicating symptoms across specialists, frustration with normal/non-attributed test results, feeling nothing more can be done) to prioritize design features of multidisciplinary 'one-stop-shop' long COVID clinics.

Patient advocacy groups could use the qualitative themes (provider disbelief, self-advocacy burden, worry about long-term cognitive/life-expectancy effects) to develop patient-facing communication guides for interactions with primary care and specialists, while explicitly noting that no cost or productivity data are available from this source.

spec.title: Long COVID Care-Coordination and Symptom-Duration Explorer (Single-Clinic Qualitative Study, n=21)
spec.boundary: This simulation represents only what a qualitative interview study of 21 adult patients at one academic post-COVID recovery clinic reported: a stated range for how long severe symptoms lasted, the clinic's minimum eligibility duration, and the specialist types patients described being referred across. It contains no cost, insurance, income, or caregiving-time data from the document, because none were reported. The symptom-duration range (1-2 years) is a reported range, not a precise point estimate. The specialist-coordination-links output is an illustrative construct built for this simulator from a count of specialist types the study names; it is not a number the study itself calculated. Findings come from a single, self-selected, referral-based sample and must not be generalized to all long COVID patients.

takeaway.patient: In this study of 21 adults at one academic post-COVID recovery clinic, patients reported symptoms lasting one to two years, well beyond the three-month minimum needed to qualify for the clinic's care, and many described confusion over which specialist to tell about new or worsening symptoms. This scenario shows how much longer even the shorter end of that reported duration was than the minimum qualifying window, and illustrates how coordination can get complicated when several specialist types (such as cardiology, physical therapy, rehabilitation psychology, and speech therapy) are involved without one clear point of contact.
takeaway.care: Among the 21 patients interviewed at this academic post-COVID recovery clinic, reported symptom duration (one to two years) consistently exceeded the clinic's three-month eligibility threshold, and patients frequently described confusion about which specialist to update as they moved across referrals to cardiology, physical therapy, rehabilitation psychology, and speech therapy. The illustrative coordination-links figure here shows how quickly potential communication pathways multiply as more specialist types are added without a single coordinating role, consistent with this qualitative finding.
takeaway.policy: This qualitative interview study of 21 patients at one academic post-COVID recovery clinic reported symptom duration (one to two years) that exceeded the clinic's three-month eligibility threshold, and documented a systemic gap in long COVID care: the authors describe a shortage of providers knowledgeable about the condition and a lack of evidence-based management guidelines, with specialists addressing symptoms within their own domain without a coordinated pathway across them. This single-site, self-selected sample with no cost, income, or caregiving data cannot support cost-effectiveness or national burden estimates, and the pooled duration finding has not been checked for variation by sex, age, or race/ethnicity within this study.

patient: If your symptoms have lasted beyond an initial few months, consider asking your care team how they plan to track and share updates on your symptoms across specialists, since this study found patients often weren't sure who to tell about new problems.

If test results come back normal but symptoms persist, you may want to ask your clinician how your ongoing symptoms are being followed over time, since the study found this was a common source of frustration.
If you feel dismissed or told your symptoms aren't real, know this was a barrier other patients in this study also described, and consider seeking a clinic with specific long COVID experience.

Consider raising with your clinician whether one provider could serve as your main point of contact across specialists, since fragmented communication was a common theme patients described in this study.
care: Consider whether a dedicated care coordinator or single point-of-contact role could reduce the number of uncoordinated hand-offs implied as more specialist types are involved in a patient's referral pattern.
This study's finding of patient confusion about which specialist to update may be worth checking against your own clinic's intake and follow-up workflows.
Consider whether shared, standardized symptom-tracking documentation across referred specialties could reduce the kind of fragmentation these patients described.

This study's finding that reported symptom duration often exceeded initial eligibility windows may be worth considering when designing follow-up intervals for long COVID referral pathways, keeping in mind this is a single-site, non-representative sample.
policy: Note that this source cannot support cost-effectiveness, willingness-to-pay, or national expenditure estimates for long COVID care coordination, since it reports no cost, insurance, or productivity data; such questions require dedicated cost-of-illness or claims-based sources.

Consider whether investment in clinician training and development of evidence-based long COVID management guidelines could address the provider-knowledge shortage and guideline gap this study's authors describe.

Consider supporting disaggregated analysis by sex, age, and race/ethnicity using federal survey data such as NHIS or BRFSS, since this study's pooled symptom-duration finding was not broken down by subgroup.

Treat these findings as hypothesis-generating from one academic, referral-based, English-speaking, pre-COVID-functioning patient sample, not as population-representative evidence for policy targeting.

inputs.label: Clinic minimum symptom-duration eligibility (months)
inputs.source: The study's population description states eligibility required symptoms impacting life for at least 3 months after infection (Limitations section context, p.1299). The 1-6 month range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: Moving this answers 'how would the gap change if the clinic used a stricter or looser minimum-duration requirement than 3 months'; it affects the low-end duration-minus-eligibility output.

inputs.label: Number of distinct specialist referral types described

The 1-6 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: Moving this answers 'how does potential coordination complexity change as more specialist types are added to a referral pattern'; it drives the illustrative coordination-links output below.

outputs.label: Reported symptom-duration range width (upper minus lower bound)
outputs.interpretation: This is simply the width of the one-to-two-year symptom-duration range this study reported for its 21 interviewed patients; a wider value reflects how imprecise this qualitative range is, not a measured change in any single patient's course over time.

outputs.label: Lower-bound symptom duration minus clinic eligibility threshold (positive = even the shorter end of the reported range exceeded the minimum eligibility window; negative could not occur under the study's own criteria)
outputs.interpretation: This compares the shorter end of the study's one-to-two-year reported duration range against the three-month minimum needed to qualify for the clinic; a larger positive value means even the least-affected patients in this reported range had symptoms well beyond initial eligibility. The study does not report this comparison directly - it is this simulator's own illustrative computation from the two figures the study does report.

outputs.label: Illustrative count of potential communication links among reported specialist types (not a figure reported by the study)
outputs.interpretation: This is an illustrative calculation, not a number the study itself computed, showing how many distinct communication pathways would exist among the specialist types (for example cardiology, physical therapy, rehabilitation psychology, and speech therapy) that patients in this study described being referred to. A higher value illustrates how quickly coordination complexity can grow as more specialists are involved, consistent with the study's qualitative finding that patients felt confused about which symptoms to report to which specialist.

scenarios.goal: Checks how the duration-range width shrinks if symptoms resolved faster than this duration-skewed sample.
scenarios.description: Sets both duration bounds to an illustrative shorter range (6 and 18 months) beyond the study's reported 1–2 year range, since the authors note their sample may not represent typical symptom duration.

scenarios.label: Longer illustrative duration range
scenarios.goal: Checks how much wider the duration range could get if symptoms persisted even longer than reported.
scenarios.description: Sets both duration bounds to an illustrative wider range (6 and 30 months) extending beyond the study's reported 1–2 year range to explore a more extreme, unreported duration spread.

scenarios.label: Stricter clinic eligibility policy
scenarios.goal: Tests whether a much stricter minimum-duration eligibility rule would still have included these patients.
scenarios.description: Raises the clinic's minimum symptom-duration eligibility to an illustrative maximum of 6 months, a stricter policy than the study's actual 3-month criterion, to see if the shorter end of reported duration still clears the bar.

scenarios.label: Single specialist pathway
scenarios.goal: Shows how much simpler coordination would look with only one specialist type instead of several.
scenarios.description: Reduces the number of distinct specialist referral types to the illustrative minimum of one, showing the coordination-link count collapse compared to the four types the study actually described.

scenarios.label: Expanded specialist network
scenarios.goal: Shows how much coordination complexity could grow with more specialist types than the study described.
scenarios.description: Increases the number of distinct specialist referral types to an illustrative maximum of six, beyond the four types reported in the study, to show how communication-link burden could scale with a larger referral network.

package.documentation:
## About this simulator

This tool is built from a qualitative interview study of 21 adult patients at one academic medical center's post-COVID recovery clinic. The study explored patients' experiences seeking and receiving care for long COVID, including care-coordination confusion, frustration with normal test results, and worry about long-term health effects. It reports no direct medical costs, non-medical costs, lost income, or caregiving-time figures, so this simulator contains no cost outputs.

**Inputs.** The symptom-duration bounds (12 and 24 months) reflect the study's own stated range ('1-2 years', Limitations section, p.1299) for how long severe symptoms lasted among study participants; this is a reported range, not a precise point estimate, and the exploration bounds around each (6-18 and 18-30 months) are assumed, not from the source. The eligibility threshold (3 months) reflects the clinic's stated inclusion criterion. The specialist-referral-type count (4) reflects the specific specialist types named in the Results section (cardiology, physical therapy, rehabilitation psychology, speech therapy); its exploration range (1-6) is assumed.

**Outputs.** Two outputs compare the study's reported duration range to its eligibility threshold; these are this simulator's own illustrative computations, not comparisons the study itself makes. The third output, an illustrative count of potential communication links among specialist types, is a constructed metric meant to visualize the study's qualitative finding of care-coordination confusion - it is not a number the study calculated.

**Limitations.** This is a single-site, self-selected, referral-based sample of 21 patients; findings should not be generalized to broader long COVID populations. The study's own authors note that many participants had symptoms for 1-2 years, which 'may not be a representative cross section of all patients with long COVID.' The pooled duration finding has not been checked for variation by sex, age, or race/ethnicity within this study, even though the study separately reports the sample's sex and age distribution; federal survey data such as NHIS and BRFSS generally supports this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it. Separately, this study documents a systemic limitation in the evidence/care system itself: a shortage of providers knowledgeable about long COVID and a lack of evidence-based management guidelines, with specialists addressing symptoms within their own domain without a coordinated pathway across them. No cost, insurance, or productivity data exist in this document, so no cost conclusions can be drawn from it.
